title: Per-client rate limiting for the notes API

overview.title: Every client gets a token bucket, checked before any handler runs
overview.explanation:
The notes API had no protection against a client hammering it. This change wraps the whole mux in a `rateLimit` middleware. Each client IP owns a **token bucket**: it starts full (the *burst*), refills at a steady *rate*, and every request spends one token. An empty bucket means `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header.

Three pieces connect: `config.go` reads `RATE_LIMIT` and `RATE_BURST` and refuses bad values, `main.go` builds one `Limiter` and wraps the mux, and `ratelimit/limiter.go` does the arithmetic under a mutex. The tests pin the arithmetic with a fake clock and prove concurrent callers can't overspend.

The limiter is deliberately small: in-memory, per process, keyed by the TCP peer address. That is the right first step for a single instance, and the README says plainly where it stops working.

diagrams.caption: Over the limit, the request stops at the middleware: the handler and the store's mutex are never touched.

decisions.title: In-memory buckets, per process
decisions.choice: Buckets live in a map inside the Go process.
decisions.alternatives: A shared store such as Redis, so every replica counts against one budget.
decisions.tradeoff: Two replicas allow twice the rate, and a restart forgets every bucket. Fine for one instance; revisit before scaling out.

decisions.title: Lazy refill instead of a ticker
decisions.choice: Allow() adds rate × elapsed tokens when it runs; nothing runs between requests.
decisions.alternatives: A goroutine that tops up every bucket on a timer.
decisions.tradeoff: No background work and exact arithmetic. But buckets are never deleted, so memory grows with every distinct IP.

decisions.title: Key by RemoteAddr
decisions.choice: The client key is the TCP peer's IP.
decisions.alternatives: X-Forwarded-For, which is only safe when a trusted proxy sets it.
decisions.tradeoff: Behind a proxy every caller shares one bucket. Trusting the header without a proxy lets clients pick their own key.

overview.remember: A token bucket allows short bursts but caps the average: burst is how many at once, rate is how fast it refills.

quiz.prompt: With RATE_LIMIT=5 and RATE_BURST=10, a quiet client sends 12 requests at once. What happens?
quiz.answer: The bucket starts full at 10 tokens and nothing refills between simultaneous requests. The next token is 200 ms away, which rounds up to Retry-After: 1.

quiz.prompt: The service runs as three replicas behind a round-robin load balancer. Roughly how fast can one client go?
quiz.answer: Each process keeps its own buckets, so the client gets a full budget on every replica.

quiz.prompt: Why does Allow() take a mutex when Node code doing the same Map update wouldn't need a lock?
options: net/http serves each request on its own goroutine, so Allow() runs in parallel
The mutex makes the limiter fair
quiz.answer: Concurrent map writes in Go are a data race (and can crash the program). TestConcurrentCallersNeverOverspend runs 200 goroutines under -race to prove the lock holds.

quiz.prompt: What would a senior reviewer flag first before this ships to the public internet?
options: Buckets are never evicted, so memory grows with every distinct IP
quiz.answer: An attacker rotating source addresses creates a bucket per address. An idle-bucket sweep (or an LRU cap) is the usual fix.

files.role: Entry: wrap the whole mux once
files.explanation:
`main` now gets its settings from `loadConfig` and exits if they're invalid, rather than starting with a silent default ([fail fast](#config)).

It builds **one** limiter and wraps the entire mux ([the wrap](#wrap)). Every route, present and future, is limited by default. That is the safe default for a small API. The cost is that health checks or internal callers would be limited too; a reviewer may ask for an allowlist later.
files.remember: Middleware that wraps the mux applies to every route, including ones added later.

files.role: Settings: refuse values that would disable the limit
files.explanation:
`loadConfig` starts from defaults (5 req/s, burst 10) and overrides them from the environment ([env loop](#env)). A value that doesn't parse, or isn't positive, is an **error**, not a fallback. If `RATE_LIMIT=five` quietly fell back to "no limit", nobody would notice until the outage.

A burst below 1 is rejected separately ([burst check](#burst)): with `RATE_BURST=0.5` the bucket could never hold a whole token, and every request would get 429.

anchors.note: Burst must hold at least one token

notes.title: A map of pointers to fill a struct
notes.body: The loop ranges over name → *float64 and writes through the pointer, so one loop sets two struct fields. TypeScript objects are always references, so the same trick needs no special syntax there.

files.role: The gate: answer 429 before any handler runs
files.explanation:
`rateLimit` is a standard `http.Handler` wrapper. It asks the limiter about this client, and either passes the request on or writes the rejection itself ([the gate](#gate)). `Retry-After` must be whole seconds, so the wait is rounded **up**: 200 ms becomes 1. Rounding down would tell clients to retry immediately, into another 429.

The key is the peer IP ([client key](#key)). That is correct when clients connect directly. Behind a load balancer every request shares the balancer's IP, so all users would share one bucket. The fix is to read `X-Forwarded-For`, but only from a proxy you trust, since clients can set the header to anything.

anchors.note: The client is its TCP peer IP

notes.title: Go middleware is a function that wraps a Handler
notes.body: An http.Handler is anything with ServeHTTP. Middleware takes the next handler and returns a new one; not calling next.ServeHTTP is how it stops the chain. Express does the same with next().

files.role: The bucket: lazy refill under one mutex
files.explanation:
Each key gets a `bucket` with a token count and the time it was last touched. A new key starts **full**, so a client's first burst is allowed ([new bucket](#new)).

Refill is lazy ([refill](#refill)): instead of a timer per client, `Allow` adds `elapsed × rate` tokens, capped at the burst, whenever the key is seen. Then it spends a token or computes how long until one arrives ([spend](#spend)). The `now` field is a seam so tests can control the clock.

The whole method holds `l.mu`, because `net/http` calls it from many goroutines at once. One mutex for all keys is simple and fast enough for a small service; under heavy contention you would shard the map. The question a reviewer should ask: buckets are never deleted, so memory grows with every distinct IP. (Wall-clock jumps are not a problem: `time.Now` carries a monotonic reading, and `Sub` uses it.)

anchors.note: Refill by elapsed time, capped at burst
Spend a token, or say how long to wait

files.remember: Lazy refill means no timers: the bucket is brought up to date only when its key is used.

notes.title: Why Go needs the mutex and Node wouldn't
notes.body: Go serves requests on many goroutines in parallel, so two Allow calls can update the map at the same moment: a data race. Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, so a synchronous Map update can't interleave with another.
notes.code:
l.mu.Lock()
defer l.mu.Unlock() // runs when Allow returns
b := l.buckets[key]
b.tokens--

notes.title: Returning two values
notes.body: Go functions can return several values; callers destructure them like a TypeScript tuple. Here the second value is the wait, meaningful only when the first is false.

files.role: Proof: the arithmetic and the lock
files.explanation: A fake clock pins the burst-then-refill arithmetic (the 4th request waits exactly 500 ms at 2 tokens/s), keys are shown to be independent, and 200 goroutines sharing one key must get exactly the burst of 50. Run it with `-race` to make the last test meaningful.
With rate 1 and burst 1, the second request gets 429 and `Retry-After: 1`. This pins the status and the rounding, the two things clients depend on.

files.role: Docs: configuration and the limits of the limiter
files.explanation: Documents the two new variables and states the honest limits: per process, forgotten on restart, and wrong behind a proxy until the key is fixed.
